302.title: The fall (CCC 390, 404–405)
302.hook: a wound handed down to all, a loss of original holiness
302.howItsDone: Catholics are taught that baptism takes away original sin, while its wound, the inclination to sin, remains, and they turn to confession and grace for healing throughout life. The Exsultet, with its felix culpa, is sung at the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, imago Dei: every human being made to the image of God. Your line was someone, not something. Whose name did you learn? Today, the question that follows: if we're God's image, why are we like this? Day three hundred two.

You know the feeling. You promised yourself you wouldn't say it, and you said it. You meant to be patient, and the moment the kid spilled the juice, you weren't. Paul, writing to the Romans, describes it better than most of us could: the good he wants to do, he doesn't do, and the thing he hates, he does. Nobody has to teach a toddler to grab. Nobody takes a class in resentment. Something in us leans the wrong way before we've chosen anything. The Church has a name for that lean, and a story for where it came from. Today, the fall.
screen: `YOU SAID IT ANYWAY.` → `NOBODY TEACHES A TODDLER TO GRAB.` → `WHERE DOES THE LEAN COME FROM?`

segments.voice: First, the story. In Genesis 3, the first man and woman live in friendship with God in the garden. The serpent asks a question that plants doubt, and they reach for the one fruit they were told to leave. Then they hide. The Catechism says the account uses figurative language, but that it tells of a real event at the beginning of human history: the first people chose themselves over God. Second, what was lost. The Church calls it original holiness and justice: a harmony with God, inside the person, between man and woman, and with creation. Paul sums up the result in the Douay-Rheims: "Wherefore as by one man sin entered into this world, and by sin death." Third, the key distinction. Original sin, the Catechism teaches, is not something you did. It is contracted, not committed. It's a state we're born into, not a personal fault. No baby is guilty of anything it chose. Fourth, how deep it goes. Here the Catholic word is careful. Human nature is not totally corrupted. It is wounded: weakened in its powers, subject to ignorance, suffering and death, and inclined to sin. That inclination has an old name, concupiscence. Christians describe this in different ways: Orthodox Christians often speak of ancestral sin, and many Reformed Protestants of a deeper corruption of nature. The Catholic Church says wounded. And on Easter night, the Church sings an old Latin hymn that dares to call Adam's sin a happy fault, felix culpa, because of the one it brought to rescue us. So the story Catholics tell is not about how bad we are. It's about a wound that can be healed.
screen: `THEY REACHED, THEN HID.` · `ORIGINAL HOLINESS, LOST.` · `CONTRACTED, NOT COMMITTED.` · `WOUNDED, NOT TOTALLY CORRUPTED.` · then, large: `O FELIX CULPA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with human weakness. Settle, and breathe. Think of one weakness of yours, a place where you lean the wrong way, again and again. Don't defend it, and don't beat yourself up. Just look at it the way a good doctor looks at a wound: honestly, and with care. Then think of someone else's weakness, one that grates on you. Look at it the same way. Wounded, not ruined. If you pray, you can ask for healing, for them and for you. The bell holds the time.
Original sin. Not a sin you committed, but a wound handed down to every human being from the beginning: the loss of original holiness, and a lean toward sin. Today's word.
Your line: wounded, not ruined. Today, when you or someone near you gets it wrong, say the line in your head before you say anything out loud. Day three hundred two.

303.title: The Word was made flesh (CCC 456–460)
303.hook: God became human to save us, show us love, and share his life
303.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass, Catholics bow during the Creed at the words about the Incarnation, and on Christmas and the Annunciation they genuflect at those words instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, original sin: a wound handed down, not a crime committed. Your line was wounded, not ruined. Did you say it in your head before you said anything out loud? Today, the Church's answer to the wound. Day three hundred three.

Sunday Mass. The whole church is standing, saying the Creed together, words that are easy to say on autopilot. And then, in the middle, a strange thing happens. At one line, heads go down. People bow. On Christmas and on the feast of the Annunciation, they do more: they drop to one knee, right there in the pew, in the middle of a sentence. Kids who don't know why do it because the grown-ups do. The line is about God doing something no one expected. Today, the Word made flesh.
screen: `THE CREED, ON AUTOPILOT.` → `EVERY HEAD GOES DOWN.` → `ONE KNEE, MID-SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: The line is this: and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man. First, the word. Incarnate comes from the Latin caro, carnis: flesh. It's the same root as carnivore and chili con carne. Incarnation means, bluntly, God in meat and bone. John's Gospel says it in the Douay-Rheims: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." The Word is the eternal Son, who was with God and was God. And he took flesh. Second, why. The Catechism gives four reasons, and they're worth counting on your fingers. One: to save us, by reconciling us with God. Two: so that we might know God's love, which John says was shown by God sending his Son. Three: to be our model of holiness, a life you can actually watch. Four: to make us, in the words of Second Peter, partakers of the divine nature. Third, that last one surprises people. The Catechism quotes Athanasius, a bishop of Alexandria, who put it in one bold line: the Son of God became man so that we might become God. Theologians call it divinization, and it doesn't mean we stop being creatures. It means God's life can be given to us. Fourth, the name. Matthew's Gospel calls the child Emmanuel, and explains it: "which being interpreted is, God with us." Not God above us, looking down. God with skin. God who got hungry, tired, and thirsty. That's why heads bow in the Creed: it's the moment Catholics remember that the distance between God and us was crossed from God's side.
screen: `CARO: FLESH.` · `SAVE, SHOW LOVE, MODEL, SHARE.` · `THAT WE MIGHT SHARE GOD'S LIFE.` · `EMMANUEL: GOD WITH US.` · then, large: `AND THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow at the words. Settle, and breathe. If you know the Creed, say it slowly to yourself, and when you reach was incarnate, bow your head, or, if you're able and it feels right, go down on one knee, the way the Church does at Christmas. If you don't know the Creed, just say the six words: and the Word was made flesh. Then stay there. Notice your own flesh: your hands, your breath, the weight of your body. That's what Catholics say God took on. The bell holds the time.
Incarnation. From the Latin for flesh: the Son of God taking a real human body and soul, to save us, show us love, and share his life. Today's word.
Your line: god with skin. Today, when you eat, or get tired, or get thirsty, remember the Church's claim that God has felt it too. Day three hundred three.

304.title: True God and true man (CCC 464–469)
304.hook: fully God and fully human, not a mixture
304.howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed that Christ is true God and true man, and some meditate on his human feelings in the Gospels, especially in Lent and in the Sorrowful Mysteries of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Incarnation: the Word made flesh. Your line was god with skin. Did you get hungry, or tired, and remember? Today, the question it raises: how can one person be both? Day three hundred four.

One person, both God and human. The mind reaches for a shortcut. Maybe he was God wearing a human costume, like a king in disguise. Maybe he was a very holy man God adopted. Maybe he was half and half, like a centaur, or a blend, like coffee with milk, where you can't find either one anymore. Versions of those shortcuts were tried in the early Church, and argued over in councils and letters. And the Church said no to them. What it said instead fits in five words.
screen: `A KING IN DISGUISE?` → `HALF AND HALF?` → `COFFEE WITH MILK?`

segments.voice: The five words: true God and true man. First, not part and part. The Catechism is plain: Jesus is not partly God and partly human, and not a confused mixture of the two. He is fully both. Second, the councils. In the year 451, bishops met at Chalcedon and wrote the careful version: one person, the Son of God, in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Four withouts, each one closing a door on a shortcut. Some ancient churches, like the Coptic and Armenian churches, have put the faith in different words, and in recent decades their leaders and the popes have signed statements saying they share the same faith in Christ. Third, what fully human means. It means a human body, and also a human mind that learned, and a human will, and human feelings. The Gospels don't hide them. In Mark, he looks around at people "with anger, being grieved for the blindness of their hearts." A rich man runs up and kneels before him, and Mark says Jesus looked at him and loved him. In the garden, he says: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." And at his friend Lazarus's tomb, in John, three plain words:"And Jesus wept." Fourth, why it matters on a Tuesday. The letter to the Hebrews says Christians don't have a high priest who can't feel what they feel, but "one tempted in all things like as we are, without sin." The loneliness, the grief, the anger at unfairness, the dread before something hard. Catholics say none of it is foreign to him.
screen: `NOT PART AND PART. NOT A BLEND.` · `CHALCEDON, 451: FOUR WITHOUTS.` · `ANGER, LOVE, SORROW, TEARS.` · `TEMPTED IN ALL THINGS, WITHOUT SIN.` · then, large: `AND JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice his human emotions. Settle, and breathe. Pick one of the four moments: the anger at hard hearts, the love for the rich man, the sorrow in the garden, the tears at the tomb. Picture it. His face. Then find the same feeling somewhere in your own week. When were you angry at something unfair? When did grief catch you? Set your moment next to his. If you pray, you can talk to him about it, as someone who knows. The bell holds the time.
True God and true man. The Church's five words for Jesus: one person, fully divine and fully human, not a mixture and not a disguise. Today's word.
screen: `TRUE GOD AND TRUE MAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he felt what you feel. Today, when a strong feeling hits, name it, and remember one Gospel moment when he felt it too. Day three hundred four.

305.title: The Paschal mystery (CCC 571)
305.hook: his death and resurrection as one saving event
305.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Paschal mystery above all in the Easter Triduum, from Holy Thursday evening through Easter Sunday; at the Easter Vigil the Paschal candle is blessed, marked with a cross, alpha and omega, the year and five grains of incense, and lit from a new fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday, true God and true man: one person, fully both. Your line was he felt what you feel. Which Gospel moment did you set beside your own? Today, what he went through for it. Day three hundred five.

Late on Holy Saturday night, a Catholic church is completely dark. Outside, a fire is burning in a small iron bowl. A priest cuts a cross into a tall new candle, and the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and the numbers of the year. He may press five grains of incense into it, for five wounds. Then the candle is lit from the fire and carried into the dark church, and one by one, everyone's small candle is lit from it, until the whole room is gold. A cross, wounds, and light, all on one candle. Today, why Catholics refuse to separate them.
screen: `A DARK CHURCH. A FIRE OUTSIDE.` → `A CROSS CUT INTO A CANDLE.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM GOES GOLD.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Paschal comes from pascha, the Greek form of the Hebrew pesach: Passover. Jesus died at Passover, and the first Christians read his death through it. Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." The lamb whose blood marked the doors in Egypt, the night of passing from slavery to freedom: Christians saw Jesus as that lamb, and his death and rising as that passage. Second, one event, not two. The Catechism calls the cross and the resurrection together the Paschal mystery, and puts it at the center of the Good News. Good Friday isn't a sad chapter followed by a happy one. The death and the rising are one saving act: through death to life. That's why the liturgy treats Holy Thursday evening to Easter Sunday as one great celebration, the Triduum, the three days. Third, mystery. In Catholic language a mystery isn't a puzzle to be solved. It's something true and so deep you can keep entering it your whole life without reaching the bottom. Fourth, the pattern. Jesus gave it a picture before it happened: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Catholics say the Paschal mystery isn't only something that happened to him. Through baptism, they are drawn into it, and they recognize its shape in their own lives: the endings that turn out to be passages, the losses that bring forth fruit. Not every sorrow feels that way while you're in it. The Church doesn't pretend it does. It points at the candle: the cross is still on it, even in the light.
screen: `PASCHA: PESACH, PASSOVER.` · `ONE EVENT: THE CROSS AND THE RISING.` · `A MYSTERY YOU KEEP ENTERING.` · `THE GRAIN OF WHEAT MUST DIE.` · then, large: `CHRIST OUR PASCH IS SACRIFICED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a cross and a candle. If you have a crucifix and a candle nearby, set them side by side. If not, picture them. Settle, and breathe. Look at the cross for a few breaths. Then the light. Then both at once. Now think of one ending in your own life that later became a beginning: a move, a loss, a no that led somewhere. Let it sit between the two. If you pray, you can thank God for it. The bell holds the time.
Paschal mystery. Christ's death and resurrection as one saving passage, named for the Passover, and at the center of the Catholic faith. Today's word.
Your line: through death to life. Today, when something ends, even something small, ask what it might be a passage into. Day three hundred five.

306.title: If Christ be not risen (1 Corinthians 15:14; CCC 639)
306.hook: Catholics hold the resurrection happened, not as a metaphor
306.howItsDone: Catholics profess every Sunday in the Creed that Christ rose on the third day, celebrate the resurrection for the fifty days of Easter, and in many communities, especially Eastern Catholic ones, greet each other at Easter with Christ is risen, and the reply, he is truly risen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Paschal mystery: the cross and the rising as one passage. Your line was through death to life. What ended for you, and what might it lead into? Today, the second half of that passage, and one very blunt sentence. Day three hundred six.

Word reaches the man who founded the church in Corinth: some of its members are saying the dead don't really rise. He could soften it. Say the story is beautiful, whatever happened. Say what matters is what Jesus taught. Instead he writes one of the bluntest sentences you could put in a letter. If it didn't happen, he says, our preaching is empty, and so is your faith. He bets the whole thing on one event. The writer is Paul. The letter is First Corinthians. And the Catholic Church still stands behind his bet.
screen: `SOME SAY THE DEAD DON'T RISE.` → `HE DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` → `HE BETS EVERYTHING ON ONE EVENT.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "And if Christ be not risen again, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." Vain: empty. No resurrection, no faith worth having. Paul goes further: if Christ isn't raised, Christians are still in their sins, and if their hope is for this life only, they are of all people the most miserable. Second, the witnesses. Just before this, Paul lists who saw the risen Jesus: Cephas, that's Peter, then the apostles, then more than five hundred people at once, many of whom, he says, are still alive. That last detail reads like an invitation: go and ask them. And Paul says he is handing on what he himself received, so the list was already being passed along before he wrote it down. Third, what the Church teaches. The Catechism calls the resurrection a real event, with manifestations that were historically witnessed, as the New Testament shows. Not a metaphor for the disciples' hope. Not a way of saying his teaching lived on. The tomb was empty, and he was seen. And the Catechism points out that the disciples were not easy believers: they thought the women's report was nonsense, and Thomas refused to believe unless he could touch the wounds. Fourth, what kind of rising. Not a return to the old life, the way Lazarus came back and would later die again. Catholics say Jesus rose into a glorified life that death can't touch, still bearing the wounds, able to eat with friends, and no longer bound by locked doors. And in Matthew, the angel at the empty tomb answers Paul's if in three words: he is risen.
screen: `IF NOT, OUR FAITH IS VAIN.` · `MORE THAN FIVE HUNDRED AT ONCE.` · `A REAL EVENT, NOT A METAPHOR.` · `NOT LAZARUS: A GLORIFIED LIFE.` · then, large: `HE IS RISEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say he is risen. Settle, and breathe. Picture the early morning: the stone rolled back, the women running, Peter running after them. Then, quietly, say the three words: he is risen. Say them again, slower. Notice what happens in you. Maybe joy, maybe doubt, maybe both. Thomas had doubt, and he's a saint. Whatever you feel, let it be honest. If you pray, you can bring the doubt and the joy to God together. The bell holds the time.
If Christ be not risen. Paul's blunt sentence: without the resurrection, the faith is empty. Catholics hold that it happened. Today's word.
screen: `IF CHRIST BE NOT RISEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he is risen. Today, say it once, out loud or in your head, somewhere ordinary: the car, the sink, the line at the store. Day three hundred six.

307.title: The Holy Spirit (CCC 683–690)
307.hook: the advocate and comforter, the breath of the Church
307.howItsDone: Catholics call on the Holy Spirit with the prayer that begins come, Holy Spirit, and with the hymns Veni Creator Spiritus and Veni Sancte Spiritus; they celebrate the Spirit's coming at Pentecost and receive the Spirit's gifts in confirmation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, if Christ be not risen: Paul's bet on one event. Your line was he is risen. Where did you say it? Today, what the risen Jesus gives his friends when they're hiding behind a locked door. Day three hundred seven.

Picture a courtroom. You're the one on trial, and you don't speak the language. Everyone is talking fast, the papers make no sense, and you're completely alone. Then someone walks in, sits down next to you, puts a hand on your shoulder, and says: I'm with you. I'll speak for you. Hold on to that picture. The night before he died, Jesus promised his friends someone exactly like that. He used a Greek word from the courtroom. And after he rose, he gave that someone to them in the most intimate way imaginable: with his own breath.
screen: `ALONE IN A COURTROOM.` → `SOMEONE SITS DOWN BESIDE YOU.` → `GIVEN WITH A BREATH.`

segments.voice: First, the promise. At the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "And I will ask the Father, and he shall give you another Paraclete, that he may abide with you for ever." Paraclete is the Greek parakletos: someone called to your side. In a law court, an advocate. In grief, a comforter. English Bibles have tried both words, and neither holds all of it. Notice the word another. Jesus has been their Paraclete. Now there will be a second one, who won't leave. Second, the breath. On Easter evening the disciples are behind locked doors, afraid. Jesus stands among them, and John says "he breathed on them; and he said to them: Receive ye the Holy Ghost." In both Hebrew and Greek, the word for spirit is also the word for breath and wind: ruach, pneuma. The first breath of the Bible is God breathing life into the first human. Here the risen Jesus breathes again, and a new creation starts. Third, how the Spirit is known. The Catechism says the Spirit is the one who lets anyone say Jesus is Lord at all, and yet he doesn't speak of himself. Catholics say they know him by what he does: in the Scriptures he inspired, in the sacraments, in prayer, in the gifts given to ordinary believers, and in the lives of the saints. Fourth, the breath of the Church. The Son and the Spirit, the Catechism says, are always sent together. You don't get one without the other. Catholics say the Spirit is the reason the Church is alive at all, the way breath is the reason a body is.
screen: `ANOTHER PARACLETE, FOR EVER.` · `HE BREATHED ON THEM.` · `KNOWN BY WHAT HE DOES.` · `THE SON AND THE SPIRIT, SENT TOGETHER.` · then, large: `RECEIVE YE THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: come, Holy Spirit. Settle, and notice your breath without changing it. In, out. Every breath you've ever taken was given, not made. If you pray, you can use a very old short prayer to the Spirit, just three words, one on each slow breath: come, Holy Spirit. If you don't pray, simply breathe, and think of someone who once sat down beside you when you were alone. The bell holds the time.
Paraclete. From the Greek for one called to your side: the advocate and comforter, the Holy Spirit Jesus promised would stay. Today's word.
Your line: the breath of god. Today, three times, when you notice your breathing, let it remind you that you're not the only one breathing in you. Day three hundred seven.

308.title: Grace (CCC 1996–2005)
308.hook: a free gift, God's own life shared with us
308.howItsDone: Catholics believe sanctifying grace is first given in baptism and is restored and strengthened through the sacraments, especially confession and the Eucharist; some also pray for the actual graces they need for a particular day or task.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Paraclete: the one called to your side, given with a breath. Your line was the breath of god. Did your breathing remind you? Today, what that breath brings with it. Day three hundred eight.

Someone pays for your coffee in the drive-through line, and drives off before you can thank them. What happens next varies. Some people want to pay it back, or pay it forward right away, or explain why they didn't really need it. A gift that can't be repaid takes the account out of our hands. Hold on to that moment. It sits close to the center of today's teaching. Catholics say the life of God in the soul is exactly that kind of gift.
screen: `SOMEONE PAYS FOR YOUR COFFEE.` → `PAY IT BACK? PAY IT FORWARD?` → `A GIFT YOU CAN'T REPAY.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Grace is the Latin gratia, and you can hear its cousin in gratis: free. The Greek is charis, a gift freely given. Paul says it in the Douay-Rheims: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." Second, what the gift is. The Catechism calls grace favor: the free and undeserved help God gives. But then it goes further. Grace is a share in God's own life. Not a thing God hands over from a distance. God giving himself. Third, two kinds. The Church speaks of sanctifying grace, a lasting gift that makes a person holy and friends with God, first given in baptism, and it's today's word. And it speaks of actual graces: God's help in particular moments, the nudge to call someone, the strength to hold your tongue. One is like the life of a tree. The other is like the rain on a given day. Fourth, earning. Since the Reformation, Catholics and Protestants have argued about grace and merit, sometimes bitterly. In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration saying together that people are accepted by God by grace alone, in faith in Christ, not because of any merit of their own. Catholics still speak of merit, and the Catechism explains that even merit is itself God's gift. A prayer of the Mass, drawing on Augustine, puts it this way: when God crowns our merits, he is crowning his own gifts.
screen: `GRATIA, GRATIS: FREE.` · `A SHARE IN GOD'S OWN LIFE.` · `THE TREE'S LIFE, THE DAY'S RAIN.` · `1999: BY GRACE ALONE, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `IT IS THE GIFT OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive one gift without earning it. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something good in your life that you did nothing to deserve. The family you were born into, a friend who stayed, your eyes, this morning's light. Don't explain it. Don't plan how to pay it back. Just receive it, the way you'd open your hands. If you pray, you can simply say thank you. The bell holds the time.
Sanctifying grace. The lasting gift of God's own life, first given in baptism, that makes a person holy and a friend of God. Free, not earned. Today's word.

Your line: free, not earned. Today, when someone does something kind for you, don't pay it back right away. Just say thank you, and let it be a gift. This week ran from the fall to the Word made flesh, true God and true man, the Paschal mystery, the resurrection, the Spirit, and now grace. Day three hundred eight.
